title: Encoder vs. Decoder vs. Encoder-Decoder
oneLineScope: When and why to pick each of the three transformer families — encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder — and how T5's text-to-text framing tried to unify them.
prose:
By 2019, three distinct families of transformer had established themselves, each derived from the same attention machinery but oriented toward different tasks by a combination of architecture and training objective. Understanding which to reach for — and why — requires holding the structural differences in view alongside the tasks each is naturally suited to. This node assembles that comparison from the pieces developed in the preceding nodes.

The three families

Encoder-only (the BERT family): a stack of \(L\) full-attention transformer blocks with no causal mask. Every position attends to every other; the output is a sequence of dense contextual representations, one per token. Pre-trained with the masked LM objective (and, in BERT's original formulation, NSP — later found dispensable by RoBERTa). Naturally suited to understanding tasks: classification, named-entity recognition, extractive question answering — anywhere you need to map a fixed input to a label or a selected span. Cannot generate sequences autoregressively: with full bidirectional attention there is no principled way to decode token by token without reconstructing the masking at inference time.

Decoder-only (the GPT family): a stack of \(L\) transformer blocks with a causal (lower-triangular) mask. Each position attends only to its predecessors. Pre-trained with the next-token cross-entropy objective. Naturally suited to generation and in-context learning: open-ended text production, completion, and — at large scale — few-shot adaptation by prepending examples to the prompt. Cannot efficiently encode a complete bidirectional context for classification tasks (though it can be fine-tuned to do so).

Encoder-decoder (the original Vaswani et al. 2017 transformer, T5, BART): a full encoder reads the source sequence with bidirectional attention; a causal decoder generates the target, attending to the encoder's output via cross-attention at each layer. Pre-trained with either span-corruption objectives (T5) or denoising objectives (BART). Naturally suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks: machine translation, abstractive summarization, question generation — anywhere the output is a new sequence conditioned on a complete input sequence.

T5 and the text-to-text framing

Raffel et al. (2020) — T5, "Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer" — proposed an elegant unification: cast every NLP task as a sequence-to-sequence problem with text input and text output. Translation becomes "translate English to German: sentence"; sentiment becomes "sentiment: sentence" → "positive" or "negative"; summarization becomes a straight seq2seq. By using one architecture (encoder-decoder), one objective (span corruption: replace contiguous spans with sentinel tokens and predict the missing spans in the decoder), and one loss function across all tasks, Raffel et al. could do large-scale controlled comparisons of architecture choices, pre-training objectives, and dataset compositions on the same footing. T5 was trained on C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus), a filtered version of Common Crawl totaling roughly 750 GB of text. The text-to-text framing is conceptually clean; whether it is efficient — using a full encoder-decoder to predict a single-word sentiment label — is a legitimate question, one T5 does not fully answer.

BART (Lewis et al., 2019) took a different approach to the encoder-decoder: pre-train by corrupting the input in various ways (token masking, deletion, permutation, text infilling) and training the decoder to reconstruct the original. BART proved especially effective on summarization and generative question answering, where the ability to reconstruct corrupted text transfers well to generating fluent output conditioned on a noisy or incomplete source.

The historical arc

From roughly 2018 to 2020, encoder-only models (BERT, RoBERTa) dominated NLU benchmarks, and encoder-decoder models dominated seq2seq tasks. The decoder-only lineage was competitive on generation but seemed architecturally specialized. The arc shifted as scale arrived: decoder-only models at billion-parameter scale, trained on web-scale corpora, showed that in-context learning — adapting to new tasks by reading examples in the prompt, with no weight updates — was an emergent capability tied to model size rather than to architectural bidirectionality. GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) demonstrated this at scale, and the decoder-only paradigm became dominant for general-purpose language models. The encoder-decoder family retained a strong niche in structured generation tasks. The encoder-only family remains the standard for embedding-based retrieval and NLU. Those later developments — scaling laws, in-context learning — are the subject of subsequent nodes in this graph, and the tokenization choices that all three families depend on are the subject of the node immediately ahead.

diagrams.caption: Three side-by-side mini-architectures showing the characteristic attention pattern of each transformer family: encoder-only (bidirectional), decoder-only (causal), and encoder-decoder (both).
diagrams.altText: Three columns side by side. Left column labeled 'Encoder-only (BERT)': a stack of blocks with a full grid of bidirectional self-attention arrows among all token positions. Middle column labeled 'Decoder-only (GPT)': a stack of blocks with a lower-triangular causal mask, only leftward arrows. Right column labeled 'Encoder-decoder (T5, Vaswani)': an encoder stack with bidirectional attention feeding via cross-attention into a decoder stack with causal attention. Each column labels its attention pattern and a representative model name.
diagrams.prompt: Structural side-by-side diagram of the three transformer families, three columns. Left column labeled 'Encoder-only (BERT)': a small stack of two or three block rectangles. Inside, draw a 4-by-4 grid of dots representing the attention matrix — all cells filled, no masking, labeled 'bidirectional: all attend to all'. Below the stack, a label '[CLS] → classification'. Middle column labeled 'Decoder-only (GPT)': same small stack of blocks. Inside, a 4-by-4 lower-triangular attention grid — only the lower triangle and diagonal filled, upper triangle empty/grey, labeled 'causal: left context only'. Below, a label 'next-token generation'. Right column labeled 'Encoder-decoder (T5, original Transformer)': two stacked sub-groups — an upper encoder section with a full bidirectional grid, and a lower decoder section with a lower-triangular grid plus a cross-attention connection (a double arrow) from the encoder output to the decoder. Below, a label 'seq2seq: translation, summarization'. Under each column, list one or two representative model names in muted grey. Keep it clean with generous spacing; structural diagram.
